claims.claim_vi: Workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; agents are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own process and tool use.
Agents are typically LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop, and need ground truth from the environment at each step.
Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance and can compound errors; simplest solution first.
claims.section: When (and when not) to use agents

claims.claim_vi: Agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints, and stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations maintain control.
An agent can have memory for preferences and knowledge, and a system can be single-agent, multi-agent or human-machine.
claims.verified_by: Carried from the source as general description; not independently checked.

design_notes_vi: Vòng lặp dọc có mũi tên quay lại; thẻ dừng nêu ba điều kiện. Chọn ví dụ đặt lịch họp tự nghĩ ra. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: Source lists five agent types (simple reflex, model-based reflex, goal-based, utility-based, learning); not needed for the main idea and not verified, so omitted.

The lesson scopes the word agent to LLM agents (language-model agents with a tool loop); agents in the broad AI sense, such as simple-reflex agents, need neither a language model nor a tool loop and are only mentioned as out of scope.
Source defines an agent by its capabilities only; the lesson adds the cost and error trade-off and the workflow-versus-agent distinction from Anthropic.
